Cybersecurity Company Intelligence — Batch 1 (Apple → AMD)

Cybersecurity Company Intelligence — Batch 1

Coverage: 2016 → September 2026

Purpose: Cybersecurity-focused historical intelligence on the first 10 companies from the master company list. Emphasis is on major technology/feature changes, security architecture evolution, significant vulnerability themes/incidents, bug bounty/security programs, attack surface, and research priorities.

1. Apple

Major evolution

  • 2016–17: iOS/macOS security foundations continued around sandboxing, code signing, Keychain, encryption and hardware-backed security.
  • 2017: APFS became an important filesystem foundation on Apple platforms.
  • 2019: macOS Catalina strengthened system separation and application permissions.
  • 2020: Apple Silicon integrated hardware and platform security more tightly.
  • 2021: iCloud+ privacy features expanded, including Private Relay and Hide My Email.
  • 2022: Lockdown Mode introduced for users facing highly sophisticated targeted attacks.
  • 2023: Rapid Security Responses enabled faster deployment of selected security fixes.
  • 2024 onward: Private Cloud Compute made cloud AI processing a major privacy/security architecture topic.

Key vulnerability themes

  • WebKit memory corruption and browser exploitation
  • kernel privilege escalation
  • sandbox escapes
  • code-signing / entitlement abuse
  • iMessage and zero-click attack chains
  • baseband, Bluetooth, AirDrop and system-service vulnerabilities

Major research themes

WebKit → Safari → XPC → sandbox → kernel → device compromise

Bug bounty / security program

Research areas include iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, Safari/WebKit, iCloud, Secure Enclave, kernel, baseband and hardware.

Primary source

https://support.apple.com/en-us/100100

2. Microsoft

Major evolution

  • 2016–17: Windows 10 security and Windows Defender/Defender ATP matured.
  • 2017: WannaCry demonstrated the operational impact of unpatched Windows networking vulnerabilities.
  • 2018: Spectre/Meltdown mitigations affected Windows and enterprise environments.
  • 2019–21: Azure, identity, Exchange and endpoint security expanded rapidly.
  • 2021: Windows 11 introduced additional hardware-backed and virtualization-based security expectations.
  • 2022–23: Microsoft Sentinel, Defender and XDR capabilities expanded.
  • 2023: Security Copilot brought generative AI into security operations.
  • 2024 onward: Secure Future Initiative made security-by-design a major engineering priority.

High-impact vulnerabilities / incidents

  • WannaCry (2017): SMB/EternalBlue exploitation and wormable ransomware.
  • BlueKeep, CVE-2019-0708: Remote Desktop Services RCE.
  • Zerologon, CVE-2020-1472: Netlogon privilege escalation with domain-controller impact.
  • PrintNightmare, CVE-2021-34527: Print Spooler RCE/privilege escalation.
  • ProxyLogon / ProxyShell: Exchange Server attack chains involving internet-facing services, authentication and server compromise.

Research attack surface

  • Azure
  • Microsoft Entra ID
  • Microsoft 365
  • Exchange
  • SharePoint
  • Windows kernel
  • RDP / SMB
  • Active Directory
  • OAuth / Graph API
  • Office
  • PowerShell
  • Edge / Chromium

Primary source

https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide

3. Alphabet / Google

Major evolution

  • 2016 onward: Project Zero and Google vulnerability research became major forces in public security research.
  • 2018: Chrome Site Isolation became a key mitigation following Spectre-class research.
  • 2019 onward: hardware security keys and identity protections expanded.
  • 2020–22: Android and Pixel security research matured alongside large-scale Chrome security work.
  • 2023 onward: AI security and red teaming became increasingly important.
  • 2025: Google launched a dedicated AI Vulnerability Reward Program.

Key vulnerability themes

  • Chrome/V8 memory corruption
  • renderer exploitation
  • sandbox escape
  • browser IPC
  • Android Binder and system_server
  • Android kernel privilege escalation
  • WebView/media/Bluetooth vulnerabilities
  • cloud and identity authorization issues

Important research chains

Chrome → V8 → renderer → IPC → sandbox → kernel

Android → Binder → system_server → SELinux → kernel

Bug bounty

Google's Bug Hunters program spans Chrome, Android and other products.

Primary source

https://bughunters.google.com/

4. Amazon / AWS

Major evolution

  • 2016 onward: Lambda/serverless and cloud security controls expanded rapidly.
  • 2018–20: IAM, cloud logging, encryption and security services matured.
  • 2019 onward: Nitro architecture became an important isolation/security layer.
  • 2020–24: cloud identity and workload security became central enterprise priorities.
  • 2023 onward: generative AI services such as Amazon Bedrock added a new security layer around model and data access.
  • 2025–26: AI infrastructure and cloud security increasingly converged.

Core attack surface

  • IAM
  • STS
  • role assumption
  • trust policies
  • resource policies
  • S3
  • EC2
  • Lambda
  • API Gateway
  • Cognito
  • KMS
  • Secrets Manager
  • EKS/ECS
  • CloudTrail
  • metadata services

Major security concept

SSRF → instance metadata → temporary credentials → AWS API access → privilege escalation

2019 Capital One breach: widely studied as an example involving SSRF, cloud credentials and S3 data access.

Research priority

Cloud security = identity security. Study cross-account trust, IAM policy evaluation, role chaining and resource-policy interactions.

Primary source

https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/

5. Meta Platforms

Major evolution

  • 2016 onward: Facebook bug bounty and account-security programs matured.
  • 2018: Cambridge Analytica became a defining privacy, authorization and third-party-app security event.
  • 2019 onward: automated security analysis scaled substantially.
  • 2021 onward: data-abuse/scraping and application-security programs expanded.
  • 2023 onward: AI security became a significant research domain across Meta products.
  • 2024–26: Llama/AI, social platforms and identity/security increasingly intersected.

Key vulnerability themes

  • OAuth and access-token problems
  • session/account takeover
  • Graph API authorization
  • IDOR / object-level authorization
  • privacy leaks
  • third-party application access
  • mobile application flaws

Defensive security research

Meta's Zoncolan static-analysis system was designed to analyze the massive codebase and identify potentially dangerous patterns at scale.

Bug bounty

Meta has operated a large public vulnerability-reporting program since 2011 and also runs specialized security/data-abuse initiatives.

Research attack surface

OAuth → Graph API → authorization → privacy → account takeover/data exposure

Primary source

https://engineering.fb.com/category/security/

7. Oracle

Major evolution

Oracle's security ecosystem spans Oracle Database, WebLogic, Java, Fusion Middleware, E-Business Suite, PeopleSoft, MySQL, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and enterprise applications.

Patch model

Oracle's long-running Critical Patch Update process follows a quarterly cycle, traditionally in January, April, July and October, with additional security alerts/patches as needed.

High-value vulnerability themes

  • Java deserialization and sandbox issues
  • WebLogic RCE, deserialization, SSRF and authentication problems
  • database privilege and authentication flaws
  • ORDS / API issues
  • middleware vulnerabilities
  • enterprise-application authorization flaws

Major reference event

Log4Shell, CVE-2021-44228: a third-party Log4j vulnerability with broad enterprise impact, including affected Oracle environments and products.

Research priority

WebLogic → Java → deserialization → RCE

Oracle DB → authentication → privilege → SQL/PLSQL → data access

Primary source

https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/

9. Intel

Major evolution

Intel's security story is heavily shaped by microarchitectural vulnerabilities as well as traditional software/firmware security.

Major security milestones

  • 2016–17: speculative-execution research intensified.
  • 2018: Spectre and Meltdown fundamentally changed CPU security.
  • 2019: MDS/ZombieLoad-class transient-execution attacks expanded the threat model.
  • 2020–22: SGX and trusted-execution-environment research expanded.
  • 2023: Downfall, CVE-2022-40982, added another major transient-execution/data-sampling case.
  • 2024–26: continued research into TEEs, side channels, firmware and confidential-computing security.

Vulnerability themes

  • speculative execution
  • cache side channels
  • branch prediction
  • transient execution
  • SGX enclave attacks
  • firmware
  • platform-management components

Research priority

CPU → cache → branch predictor → speculative execution → TEE → firmware

Primary source

https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/security-center/default.html

10. AMD

Major evolution

  • 2017: Ryzen and EPYC made AMD a major client/server CPU platform again.
  • 2018 onward: Spectre-class research drove processor mitigations and new security engineering.
  • 2019–22: SEV / SEV-ES research evolved into stronger confidential-computing protections.
  • 2022: SEV-SNP became a major isolation/attestation architecture.
  • 2023: Zenbleed, CVE-2023-20593, became a major AMD microarchitectural security issue.
  • 2023/24: Sinkclose, CVE-2023-31315, highlighted firmware/SMM-level security risk.
  • 2025–26: CPU, GPU, firmware and confidential-computing research continued to expand.

Key vulnerability themes

  • speculative execution
  • information disclosure
  • cache/branch side channels
  • firmware and SMM
  • hypervisor/VM isolation
  • SEV/SEV-SNP
  • graphics and driver vulnerabilities

Research priority

CPU → firmware → SMM → hypervisor → SEV-SNP → cloud VM isolation

Primary source

https://www.amd.com/en/resources/product-security.html

11. Qualcomm

Technology evolution

  • 2016–18: Snapdragon mobile SoCs, modem, GPU, DSP, WLAN and Bluetooth became major embedded security surfaces.
  • 2017–20: Snapdragon expanded across phones, IoT, automotive and always-connected PCs; proprietary drivers and firmware became important research targets.
  • 2020–22: 5G modem and FastConnect platforms expanded baseband and connectivity attack surfaces.
  • 2023–26: Snapdragon AI, automotive, edge and compute platforms expanded software, firmware and AI-related surfaces.

Major vulnerabilities / incidents

  • QuadRooter (2016): four Qualcomm Android chipset/driver vulnerabilities that could enable local privilege escalation/root access on affected devices.
  • Recurring modem/baseband memory corruption
  • WLAN/Bluetooth memory corruption
  • DSP/TEE vulnerabilities
  • Android kernel and proprietary-driver privilege escalation
  • authentication and cryptographic implementation flaws
  • automotive connectivity vulnerabilities

2026 representative records

  • CVE-2026-25289: WLAN firmware stack-based buffer overflow; remote attack vector; CVSS 9.6.
  • CVE-2026-21366: integer overflow in data network stack/connectivity; CVSS 7.8.
  • CVE-2026-24079: missing authentication for critical function in data modem.
  • CVE-2026-24080: biometrics fingerprint TA buffer-copy vulnerability; CVSS 7.8.
  • CVE-2026-25288: WLAN firmware buffer over-read; CVSS 7.4.
  • CVE-2026-24076: Bluetooth HOST buffer-copy vulnerability; CVSS 6.7.

Research attack surface

Baseband/modem → DSP/TEE → Android driver → kernel → device compromise

WLAN/Bluetooth → firmware parser → memory corruption → privilege boundary

Security source

https://www.qualcomm.com/company/product-security/bulletins

Security program

Sony operates Secure@Sony and accepts vulnerability reports for products and associated services; its vulnerability disclosure policy includes a PlayStation Bug Bounty Program.

2026 security posture

201. Mozilla

Major evolution

  • 2016–18: Firefox security engineering increasingly centered on sandboxing, site isolation, process separation, memory safety and rapid security releases.
  • 2019–21: Firefox Enhanced Tracking Protection and privacy controls expanded the browser's security/privacy boundary while Rust adoption increased in security-sensitive components.
  • 2022–24: Site isolation, WebAssembly, WebGPU, Fission and hardened browser process architecture created new security boundaries and complex IPC surfaces.
  • 2025–26: Firefox continued frequent security releases while memory safety, browser isolation and AI-assisted vulnerability discovery became increasingly important research themes.

2026 security signals

Mozilla's 2026 advisory series documents recurring high/critical classes including use-after-free, incorrect boundary conditions, information disclosure, privilege escalation and sandbox escapes. For example, MFSA 2026-67 described critical Firefox flaws including a WebAssembly invalid-pointer issue and a site-isolation/navigation issue; Mozilla's advisory index continued to list frequent Firefox, Android, iOS and Thunderbird security releases through September 2026.

Vulnerability themes

  • JavaScript/WebAssembly memory corruption
  • DOM and CSS parser flaws
  • graphics/WebRender exploitation
  • browser sandbox escape
  • IPC/process boundary failures
  • site-isolation bypass
  • extension privilege abuse

Research chain

Web content → parser/JS engine → renderer process → IPC → sandbox → privileged browser process/OS

Program / source

Mozilla maintains public security advisories and a vulnerability-reporting process.

Primary source

https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/security/advisories/

  • 2022–24: confidential computing, Ubuntu Pro, Landscape, cloud-native infrastructure and container security became more central.
  • 2025–26: AI/edge workloads, Linux kernel hardening, package supply-chain integrity and automated patching became increasingly important.

Security architecture

Ubuntu security relies heavily on Linux kernel controls, AppArmor, Secure Boot, package signing, unattended security updates, LTS maintenance and cloud-image hardening.

Vulnerability themes

Cross-company research chains worth prioritizing

Browser: Web content → parser/JS → renderer → IPC → sandbox → OS

Cloud-native: SaaS/identity → API → RBAC → Kubernetes/agent → container → node

CI/CD: Repository → config → runner → secret → cloud credential → production

Fintech: Identity → session → organization role → authorization/policy → payment object → transaction

SaaS connectors: Admin → OAuth scope → external API → sensitive data → downstream action

Security appliance: Internet-facing edge → parser/web UI → privileged service → OS → internal network

Virtualization: Management plane → identity → hypervisor → virtual device → guest/host boundary

OT/ICS: Engineering workstation → project/config → controller → protocol → physical process

Extended Research Priority Matrix — 241 → 290

  • Observability/SIEM: Splunk, New Relic, Dynatrace, PagerDuty, Sumo Logic
  • DevSecOps/Supply Chain: JFrog, Harness, GitGuardian, Sonar, Semgrep, Secure Code Warrior, Contrast Security, Veracode, Chainguard, Anchore
  • Cloud/Kubernetes Security: Sysdig, Aqua Security, Orca Security
  • Network/Zero Trust: Cato Networks, Tailscale, Teleport, Twingate, Ivanti, BeyondTrust
  • Email/External Risk: Abnormal Security, SecurityScorecard, BitSight, Recorded Future, ZeroFox
  • Crowdsourced Security: Bugcrowd, HackerOne, Synack, Censys, Coalfire
  • Secrets/Identity: 1Password, Keeper Security
  • Data/Database Infrastructure: Cockroach Labs, ClickHouse, SingleStore, PlanetScale, Hasura
  • Data Engineering/Analytics: PostHog, Airbyte, dbt Labs, Fivetran, Segment, Algolia, Amplitude
  • Developer Control Planes: Retool, LaunchDarkly

Cross-company attack chains

Observability: Application/endpoint → telemetry agent → ingestion API → tenant ACL → query/export → sensitive data

CI/CD supply chain: Repository → build config → scanner/runner → secret → artifact → deployment

Cloud security: Cloud identity → connector/API → asset inventory → policy → privileged remediation

Zero Trust: User/device identity → policy engine → broker/connector → private service → privileged session

Data integration: OAuth/credential → connector → source API → sync/transform → warehouse/destination

Developer control plane: Developer identity → project/environment → API → configuration/flag/workflow → production behavior

Database/API: Client → parser/GraphQL/SQL → authorization → query engine → storage/export
